Combine all ingredients in a blender.
Blend until velvety and smooth.
Pour into a tall glass, sprinkle extra cinnamon if desired, and enjoy chilled.
💡 Blend the night before and store in a filled-to-the-brim jar for up to 24 hours; the apple browns and separates, so shake hard before drinking. Make it 60–90 minutes pre-session for easy carbs.
💡 Load almond milk, spinach and apple first and blend before adding the ice; ice thrown in with the greens leaves fibrous flecks the blades cannot catch.
In a pot, sauté onion, garlic, carrot, and celery in olive oil until softened.
Add lentils, broth, thyme, salt, and pepper.
Simmer for 25–30 minutes until lentils are tender.
Adjust seasoning before serving warm.
💡 Cool and chill for 5 days or freeze in single portions for 3 months; the lentils thicken as they sit, so loosen with 50 ml broth when reheating on the hob.
💡 Keep the salt back until the lentils are tender; salting the broth at the start toughens their skins and can add 15 minutes to the simmer.
Arrange rice, edamame, kale, and avocado in a bowl.
In a small bowl, whisk tahini, lemon juice, olive oil, salt, and pepper.
Drizzle over the bowl and serve immediately.
💡 Pack rice, edamame and kale together for up to 3 days, but keep the tahini dressing in a small jar and slice the avocado fresh; it browns within hours.
💡 Whisk the lemon juice into the tahini before the oil; the paste seizes and looks split at first, so keep whisking and add 5 ml of water until it loosens.
Preheat your oven to 200°C, giving it enough time to fully heat so the chickpeas crisp properly.
Pat the chickpeas dry with a clean towel, then toss them in a bowl with the olive oil, paprika, cayenne, and salt, making sure every chickpea is evenly coated.
Spread them out on a baking sheet in a single layer, giving them space so they roast instead of steam.
Roast for 25–30 minutes, shaking the pan halfway through to help them crisp on all sides.
Let them cool completely on the baking sheet; they firm up as they cool, giving you that perfect crunch.
💡 Store fully cooled in a loosely covered jar at room temperature for 3 days; the fridge draws in moisture and softens them. Re-crisp in the oven at 180°C for 5 minutes if needed.
💡 Rub off and discard the loose chickpea skins while patting dry; skins trap steam, burn before the flesh crisps and are the usual cause of chewy centres.
Preheat oven to 175°C.
Whisk eggs and stir in chopped vegetables and cheese.
Pour mixture into muffin tins and bake 15–18 minutes until set.
💡 Refrigerate in an airtight tub for 4 days or freeze for 2 months; reheat one muffin at 600 W for 45 seconds and stop early, since egg goes rubbery when overshot.
💡 Bake until the centres are barely set and still wobble slightly; they carry on cooking in the tin, and eggs pushed past that point weep liquid and turn spongy.
Place the spinach at the base of your blender to ensure it fully incorporates.
Add the almond milk next so the greens begin softening in the liquid.
Add the berries, banana, chia seeds, and finally the ice.
Start blending on low to fold the greens into the fruit mixture, then increase to high for a smoother finish.
Blend for about 60–75 seconds or until the smoothie becomes velvety and chia seeds are evenly distributed.
If you prefer a thinner texture, add a splash of extra almond milk and blend again briefly.
💡 Drink within 30 minutes of finishing training, or freeze the fruit, spinach and chia as a bagged kit and blend fresh with milk and whey each morning.
💡 Let the chia sit in the almond milk for 5 minutes before blending; dry seeds stay gritty, whereas pre-soaked ones swell and thicken the shake evenly.
In a small pot, combine the quinoa, almond milk, and cinnamon. Warm over low heat until it simmers gently.
Add diced apple and maple syrup; stir and cook for about 5 minutes until the apples are tender.
Spoon into bowls, top with walnuts and chia seeds.
Serve warm, savoring the comforting aroma of cinnamon and sweetness of apples.
💡 Cook the quinoa and apple base ahead and chill for 4 days; reheat with 30 ml extra almond milk at 700 W for 90 seconds, then add walnuts and chia after warming so they stay crunchy.
💡 Keep the pot at a gentle simmer and stir every minute; almond milk scorches readily and quinoa left unstirred turns gluey and catches on the base.
Cook quinoa according to package directions and allow to cool slightly.
In a bowl, mix tuna, tomatoes, cucumber, and onion.
Add quinoa and drizzle with olive oil and lemon juice.
Season with oregano, salt, and pepper. Toss gently to combine.
Chill for 10 minutes before serving for a refreshing, light finish.
💡 Assemble up to 3 days ahead and eat chilled straight from the fridge; store the cucumber and tomatoes in a separate pot, as their juices dilute the dressing. It does not freeze.
💡 Spread the cooked quinoa on a tray to cool for 10 minutes before mixing; warm grains wilt the cucumber and turn the tuna dressing cloudy and greasy.
Mix chia seeds, coconut milk, and vanilla in a jar.
Stir well and refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight.
Top with diced mango before serving.
💡 Set in individual jars and chill for up to 5 days, adding the mango on top only when serving; frozen portions thaw overnight but turn slightly grainy.
💡 Shake the whey into the coconut milk until fully dissolved, add the chia, then stir again after 15 minutes; a second stir breaks up clumps that would leave a gelatinous lump at the base.
Preheat oven to 175°C.
In a bowl, mix oats, baking powder, and wet ingredients.
Fold in strawberries and almonds.
Spoon mixture into greased muffin tin and bake for 20–22 minutes.
Cool slightly before serving — sweet, chewy, and portable for busy mornings.
💡 Keep 4 days chilled in an airtight tub or freeze for 3 months; reheat from frozen at 700 W for 60 seconds, or eat cold from the tub.
💡 Let the oats sit in the almond milk and egg for 10 minutes before baking; unsoaked oats absorb liquid in the oven and leave the cups dry and crumbly.
Heat coconut oil in a skillet over 175°C and sauté onion until golden.
Add garlic, curry powder, and turmeric, stirring until aromatic (about 1 minute).
Add chickpeas, coconut milk, and tomatoes. Simmer for 10–12 minutes until thickened.
Serve hot over basmati rice and top with fresh cilantro.

💡 The curry chills for 4 days or freezes for 3 months; the basmati is best cooled quickly and stored in a separate tub. Reheat curry on the hob, stirring, and rice at 800 W under a damp kitchen towel.
💡 Keep the coconut milk at a gentle simmer, never a rolling boil; light coconut milk splits into oily flecks and thin liquid when boiled hard with the acidic tomatoes.
In a large bowl, combine quinoa, cabbage, carrots, peppers, and edamame.
In a separate bowl, whisk together olive oil, vinegar, honey, salt, and pepper.
Pour the dressing over the salad, toss well, and refrigerate for 10 minutes before serving.
💡 Dressed, it keeps 3 days chilled and improves overnight; the cabbage and carrot stay crisp, but do not freeze it, as the vegetables thaw limp and watery.
💡 Dissolve the honey in the vinegar before whisking in the oil; honey dropped straight into oil stays in a stubborn ball and the dressing never emulsifies.
Arrange apple slices on a plate like nachos.
Drizzle peanut butter evenly across the slices.
Sprinkle chopped almonds and coconut on top.
💡 Best assembled to order; if prepping ahead, slice the apple, toss in a little lemon juice and chill for up to 24 hours, keeping peanut butter and toppings in a separate pot.
💡 Warm the peanut butter for 10 seconds in the microwave and drizzle from a spoon held high; cold peanut butter drags the apple slices around instead of coating them.
Preheat oven to 175°C and lightly grease a muffin tin.
In a bowl, whisk together oat flour, protein powder, baking powder, and cinnamon.
In another bowl, combine eggs, applesauce, grated apple, and honey.
Stir wet ingredients into dry until just combined.
Pour batter into muffin tin and bake 18–20 minutes, until golden and set.
Cool for 5 minutes before serving. These muffins fill the air with warm cinnamon sweetness — perfect with morning tea.
💡 Cool completely before storing in an airtight tin for 3 days, or freeze for 2 months; 15–20 seconds at 800 W softens a chilled muffin without drying it.
💡 Mix the wet and dry ingredients with a few strokes only and bake without delay; protein powder batters over-stirred or left standing bake up dense and rubbery.
Place spinach, avocado, and cucumber into the blender first to form a nutrient-rich base.
Pour in coconut water and blend on medium until ingredients start breaking down.
Increase to high and blend until creamy and smooth.
Add hemp seeds and pulse briefly to mix evenly without altering the silky texture.
Pour into glasses and enjoy a green, refreshing, skin-nourishing smoothie.
💡 Drink within 20 minutes of blending; avocado oxidises fast and the smoothie turns brown and bitter within a couple of hours, even chilled. Blend fresh after training rather than in advance.
💡 Blend the coconut water and whey briefly on their own first, then add the avocado and cucumber; adding whey on top of a thick avocado base leaves floury pockets.
Heat olive oil in a skillet; add diced sweet potatoes and cook for 10–12 minutes until golden.
Add spinach and garlic powder, stir until wilted.
Sprinkle with feta and season with salt and pepper.
Serve warm for a hearty, savory breakfast.
💡 Cool the hash and chill for 4 days; reheat in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 4 minutes to re-crisp the cubes, and crumble the feta over afterwards. Freezing makes the potato mealy.
💡 Dice the sweet potato to 1 cm, spread in a single layer and leave it undisturbed for the first 4 minutes; constant stirring stops a crust forming and the cubes steam instead.
Heat olive oil in a pan and add lentils, chili powder, cumin, and salt.
Sauté for 2–3 minutes to absorb flavor.
Spoon lentil mixture into warm tortillas.
Top with lettuce and tomatoes before serving.
💡 Chill the spiced lentil filling for 4 days or freeze for 3 months; reheat in a pan with a splash of water, and store tortillas, lettuce and tomatoes separately to keep the wrap from sogging.
💡 Drain the diced tomatoes in a sieve before topping, and warm the corn tortillas in a dry pan for 20 seconds a side; cold corn tortillas crack the moment they are folded.
Steam the edamame for about 5 minutes, or just until the pods become bright green and tender, making sure they stay slightly firm.
Drain the edamame well and transfer them to a bowl while they’re still warm.
Sprinkle with sea salt, letting it cling lightly to the warm pods.
Add a small squeeze of fresh lemon juice right before serving to bring a bright, refreshing finish.
💡 Steamed edamame keeps 3 days chilled and is good eaten cold; if reheating, steam for 2 minutes rather than microwaving, and add the lemon only after warming so it stays bright.
💡 Pull the steamer off the heat the moment the pods turn vivid green; another 2 minutes and the beans go dull, mealy and lose their bite.
Place the kiwi chunks and banana in the blender first, creating a soft base for the greens.
Add the spinach and coconut milk. Blend on medium for 20–30 seconds to start breaking down the leafy greens.
Increase speed to high and continue blending until smooth and creamy, ensuring no green streaks remain.
Add the flaxseed meal and pulse 3–4 times to mix evenly without altering the silky texture.
Pour into glasses, observe the vibrant green color, and enjoy immediately for freshness.
💡 Freeze kiwi, banana and spinach together in portion bags for up to 2 months and blend from frozen with the coconut milk; ideally drink it within an hour of your session ending.
💡 Peel the kiwi thoroughly and keep the blend under 90 seconds; kiwi skin turns gritty and extended blending warms the fruit and dulls its colour.
Preheat oven to 220°C.
Toss sweet potato fries with olive oil, paprika, garlic powder, and salt.
Arrange on a baking tray and bake 20–25 minutes, flipping halfway through.
Mix Greek yogurt and lemon juice for a creamy, tangy dip.
Serve warm and enjoy the balance of sweet and savory.
💡 Chilled fries keep 3 days and re-crisp in an air fryer at 200°C for 4 minutes; keep the yogurt dip in a separate lidded pot, where it lasts 4 days.
💡 Soak the cut fries in cold water for 20 minutes and dry thoroughly before oiling; rinsing off surface starch is what lets sweet potato crisp rather than go floppy.
Cook orzo according to package instructions; drain and cool slightly.
Toss with tomatoes, basil, olive oil, salt, and pepper.
Drizzle with balsamic glaze and chill before serving.
💡 Keeps 3 days chilled; the orzo firms up in the fridge, so let it sit 10 minutes at room temperature and add 5 ml of olive oil before eating. Hold the balsamic glaze until serving.
💡 Drain the orzo, rinse briefly under cold water and toss with the olive oil while still warm; unrinsed orzo welds into a starchy block as it cools.
Preheat oven to 200°C.
Dry chickpeas thoroughly, and toss in olive oil and spices.
Spread on a baking sheet and roast for 30 minutes, shaking halfway.
💡 Cool completely on the tray, then store in a paper bag or unsealed jar for up to 4 days; an airtight lid traps residual steam and they lose their crunch by morning.
💡 Roast the dried chickpeas plain for the first 15 minutes, then toss in the oil and spices and return to the oven; paprika added at the start scorches and tastes bitter.
Add pineapple and banana into the blender first to form a fruity base.
Pour in coconut milk and add vanilla extract.
Blend on medium for 20–30 seconds, then high until creamy and uniform.
Stir in hemp seeds and pulse 3–4 times for a nutty, protein-rich texture.
Pour into glasses and enjoy immediately post-workout for natural recovery.
💡 Freeze the pineapple and banana in portion bags and blend straight from frozen with the coconut milk; consume within 30–45 minutes after training rather than storing.
💡 Pulse the hemp seeds in at the end, as instructed, rather than blending them with the base; prolonged blending grinds them into a bitter, oily sludge.
Heat olive oil in a pot and sauté onions and garlic until fragrant.
Add mushrooms and cook until softened.
Add barley, broth, salt, and pepper.
Simmer for 30 minutes or until barley is tender.
Serve warm, garnished with fresh herbs if desired.
💡 Chill for 4 days or freeze for 3 months; barley keeps swallowing broth, so expect it to thicken and add 60 ml water when reheating on the hob.
💡 Cook the mushrooms hard in a single layer until browned before adding the broth; crowding them in the pot means they boil grey and rubbery.
Preheat oven to 175°C.
Whisk eggs, milk, salt, and pepper in a bowl.
Stir in chopped vegetables.
Pour into greased mini muffin tins and bake 15 minutes or until set.
💡 Chill in an airtight tub for 4 days or freeze for 2 months; reheat two mini frittatas at 600 W for 30 seconds, checking early so the egg does not go tough.
💡 Squeeze the moisture from the chopped spinach and peppers before stirring them in; wet vegetables pool liquid beneath the egg and leave the bases watery.
In a blender, combine mango, banana, coconut milk, and protein powder.
Blend on high until creamy and smooth. If too thick, add a splash more coconut milk.
Pour into bowls and smooth the surface.
Sprinkle chia seeds, granola, and shredded coconut on top.
Enjoy immediately — cool, tropical, and perfectly refreshing.
💡 Blend and freeze the base in a shallow tub for up to a month; thaw in the fridge for 30 minutes, stir until spoonable, and add granola, chia and coconut at the table.
💡 Keep the mango and banana fully frozen and add the coconut milk a splash at a time; too much liquid at once turns a thick bowl into a thin smoothie.
Melt the chocolate in a microwave-safe bowl, heating it in 15-second bursts and stirring between each round until it becomes smooth and glossy.
Dip each strawberry halfway into the warm chocolate, allowing any excess to drip off, then place them carefully on a sheet of parchment paper.
Chill the strawberries in the refrigerator for about 15 minutes, or until the chocolate sets and becomes firm with a lovely shine.
💡 Best eaten the day they are made; chill up to 24 hours in a single layer, uncovered, since a lid traps condensation and the chocolate sweats. Do not freeze.
💡 Wash the strawberries early and dry them completely on kitchen paper before dipping; a single drop of water on the fruit makes the melted chocolate seize and slide off.
Add all ingredients to a blender.
Blend until smooth and silky.
Pour into a glass and enjoy the sunshine color and immune-boosting properties.
💡 Best drunk within 24 hours from a lidded jar in the fridge, shaken first because the mango pulp separates. For a week of portions, bag the mango and banana together and freeze.

💡 Pour the coconut water and honey in first, then the frozen mango and banana on top, so the blades catch liquid and the honey does not stick to the jug. Turmeric stains plastic, so rinse straight away.
Preheat your oven to 175°C, giving it a few minutes to heat thoroughly so the cookies bake evenly.

In a mixing bowl, combine the oats, protein powder, raisins, honey, and almond milk. Stir everything together until the mixture becomes thick and sticky, with the raisins evenly distributed throughout.
Using a spoon, drop small mounds of the mixture onto a baking tray lined with parchment, shaping them gently so they hold together.
Bake for 10–12 minutes, or until the tops turn lightly golden and the edges feel set. Let them cool slightly before enjoying.
💡 Cool fully on the tray, then store in an airtight tin for five days at room temperature or freeze for three months; a 10-second burst in the microwave softens a frozen one.
💡 Protein powder dries out and turns cookies chalky, so pull them at 10 minutes while the centres still look slightly underdone; they firm up as they cool on the tray.
In a large bowl, combine chickpeas, cucumber, tomatoes, onion, and olives.
In a small bowl, whisk olive oil, lemon juice, oregano, salt, and pepper.
Pour dressing over the salad and toss to coat evenly.
Top with feta before serving.
Chill for 10 minutes for enhanced flavor and freshness.
💡 Keeps three days chilled if you store the dressing separately and add the cucumber and feta on the day; the chickpeas, tomatoes, onion and olives can be boxed together. Do not freeze.
💡 Rinse and pat the chickpeas dry before dressing, otherwise the canning liquid waters down the lemon and oil. Salt the cucumber and drain for 10 minutes if prepping ahead.
Lay the cucumber slices flat on a clean surface, making sure they are even and sturdy enough to hold the filling.
Spread a thin layer of hummus over each slice, covering it gently but evenly.
Sprinkle the chopped bell pepper and olives on top, distributing them so each bite has a mix of flavors and colors.
Roll each cucumber slice tightly and secure with a toothpick to hold the filling in place.
Chill briefly before serving to allow the flavors to meld and the rolls to firm up slightly.
💡 Assemble no more than a day ahead and keep in a sealed box lined with kitchen paper to catch the cucumber's moisture. These are not freezer-friendly; the cucumber turns to mush.
💡 Use a vegetable peeler to shave long thin ribbons rather than knife slices; thick slices crack when rolled and thin ones stay pliable. Blot each ribbon before spreading hummus so it grips.
Add the chopped carrot to your blender first so it sits closest to the blades. This helps it break down smoothly.
Pour in the fresh orange juice and water to create enough liquid for blending.
Add the banana and grated ginger, then top with the ice.
Begin blending on low speed for about 20–30 seconds to help the carrot soften into the mixture.
Increase to high speed and blend for another 45–60 seconds until the texture becomes bright, silky, and pourable.
Taste and adjust ginger or liquid consistency as desired. Drink straight away to preserve the vitamin C.
💡 Carrot fibres separate within hours, so drink this within 12 hours of blending and shake hard first. Portion the chopped carrot, banana and ginger into freezer bags for a quick post-session blend.
💡 A domestic blender struggles with raw carrot, so grate it rather than chop and run the low-speed stage for the full 30 seconds before adding ice; otherwise you get gritty flecks.
Pour almond milk into the blender first.
Add blueberries, banana, and lavender.
Add ice last for the best texture.
Blend on high until the smoothie becomes creamy and lightly scented with lavender.
Taste and adjust lavender if you want a stronger calming note.
💡 Drink within 24 hours; the lavender flavour intensifies as it sits, so err on the light side if you blend the night before. Freeze blueberries and banana together in single portions.
💡 Grind the dried lavender with a pinch of the whey powder before it goes in, otherwise whole buds survive the blades and taste soapy. Whey and almond milk go in first.
Preheat oven to 200°C.
Toss zucchini with olive oil, breadcrumbs, Parmesan, salt, and pepper.
Spread on a baking sheet and bake for 20 minutes until golden.
💡 Best straight from the oven, but they keep two days chilled; recrisp in an air fryer at 200°C for 4 minutes rather than a microwave, which turns them limp. Not suitable for freezing.
💡 Courgette holds a lot of water, so cut into even batons, salt them for 15 minutes and pat dry before tossing with oil; wet batons steam and the Parmesan crumb slides off.
Scoop the avocado into the blender, breaking it into smaller pieces for easier blending.
Add the spinach and banana.
Pour in the almond milk and blend on medium until the greens break down.
Increase to high speed and continue blending until the mixture is smooth and creamy with no leafy specks remaining.
Add the ground flaxseed and pulse 3–4 times to mix without over-thickening.
Pour into glasses — the texture should be rich and buttery.
💡 Avocado browns quickly, so drink within a few hours or freeze immediately in a lidded portion pot for up to a month; thaw in the fridge overnight and re-blend briefly.
💡 Flaxseed swells within minutes and turns the drink to paste, so pulse it in last and drink straight away. Blend the whey into the almond milk before the avocado to avoid a gluey texture.
Place peaches and banana in the blender first to create a creamy base.
Add almond milk, almond butter, and cinnamon. Blend on medium for 20–30 seconds.
Increase to high speed and blend until silky smooth.
Pour into glasses and enjoy a naturally sweet, warming smoothie.
💡 Freeze sliced peaches and banana in 100 g bags so the shake comes out thick without ice; blended portions keep 24 hours chilled but the almond butter rises and needs a good shake.
💡 Almond butter clumps against cold fruit, so loosen it in the almond milk with the whey first, then add peaches and banana; a 20-second low-speed start stops it sticking under the blades.
In two glasses, layer coconut yogurt, granola, and mixed fruits.
Repeat the layers until the glasses are full.
Sprinkle shredded coconut on top.
Serve immediately for a refreshing, tropical start to your day.
💡 Layer the yogurt and fruit in jars up to three days ahead, but keep the granola and coconut in a separate pot and add at the table; pineapple juice softens granola within an hour.

💡 Drain the diced mango and pineapple on kitchen paper before layering, otherwise their juice pools at the bottom and the coconut yogurt turns watery. Toast the shredded coconut dry in a pan for crunch.
Spread the peanut butter evenly over each rice cake, letting it reach all the way to the edges so every bite feels creamy and satisfying.
Arrange the banana slices on top in a neat layer, then finish with a light sprinkle of cinnamon for a soft, sweet warmth.
💡 Assemble only when eating; rice cakes go soft within an hour of contact with peanut butter and banana browns. Pre-portion the peanut butter into small pots and slice the banana fresh.
💡 Spread the peanut butter right to the rim so it seals the cake against banana moisture, and lay slices in a single layer rather than stacking; stacked banana slides off on the first bite.
In a small bowl, whisk together the tahini, lemon juice, chili powder, water, and a pinch of salt until the mixture is smooth and creamy.
Adjust the consistency with a little extra water if needed, so the dip is pourable but still thick enough to coat the veggies.
Arrange your fresh veggie sticks on a plate, creating an inviting display.
Serve the tahini dip alongside the veggies, letting each stick pick up a bit of the creamy, zesty flavor.
💡 The dip keeps five days chilled in a jar and thickens as it sits, so loosen with 5 ml of water before serving. Store the carrot and cucumber sticks in a separate box of cold water.
💡 Tahini seizes and goes grainy when lemon hits it; that is normal, so keep whisking and add the water a few drops at a time until it turns pale and creamy again.
Slice the cucumber into 1.5 cm thick rounds and use a small spoon or melon baller to scoop out a small hollow in the center of each slice, being careful not to go all the way through.
Spoon a dollop of creamy hummus into each cucumber cup, filling the hollowed-out center generously.
Drizzle a little olive oil over the top of the hummus for added richness, and sprinkle with a pinch of paprika and freshly chopped parsley to add a burst of color and flavor.
💡 Hollow the cucumber rounds up to two days ahead and store cut-side down on kitchen paper, but fill with hummus within an hour of serving so the cups stay crisp. Freezing is not an option.
💡 Cut the rounds a little thicker than 1 cm and stop the melon baller a good 5 mm from the base; thin or over-scooped cups leak hummus and collapse when picked up.
Preheat oven to 175°C.
Mix all ingredients in a bowl until combined.
Drop spoonfuls onto a lined baking sheet and flatten slightly.
Bake for 12–14 minutes until golden.
💡 These stay soft, so keep them in an airtight tub for three days chilled or freeze flat on a tray then bag for two months; thaw at room temperature for 20 minutes.
💡 Use a well-spotted banana and mash it completely; underripe banana leaves the mixture too dry to bind the oats and the cookies crumble. Let the mix sit five minutes so the oats hydrate.
Add the frozen blueberries into the blender first.
Pour in the almond milk, then add the almond butter and vanilla extract.
Blend on high for 40–45 seconds until completely smooth and deeply purple.
Pause to check thickness—if too thick, add a splash more almond milk and blend again.
Pour into glasses; the result should be cool, thick, and naturally sweet.
💡 This one is built on frozen blueberries, so batch it by freezing the almond milk in ice-cube trays too; then the blend stays thick without dilution. Drink within 12 hours if chilled.
💡 Frozen berries straight from the freezer can stall the blades, so let them sit for two minutes and add the almond milk and whey before the fruit; a short low pulse breaks the ice jam.
Mix chia seeds, almond milk, honey, and vanilla in a jar.
Stir well, cover, and refrigerate for 2 hours until thickened.
Stir again before serving and top with fresh peaches.
💡 The pudding base keeps five days in sealed jars in the fridge and needs no reheating; add the diced peach on the morning you eat it so it stays firm and bright. Chia pudding does not freeze well.
💡 Chia clumps if left alone, so stir once immediately after mixing and again after 10 minutes before the long chill; that second stir prevents a solid lump at the bottom and thin milk on top.
In a bowl, mash the avocado with the lemon juice, salt, and pepper until it becomes smooth and creamy, leaving a few small chunks if you like a bit of texture.
Add the tuna to the bowl and stir it in thoroughly until the mixture is well combined and velvety.
Spoon the tuna-avocado mixture into crisp lettuce cups, filling each one generously.
Serve immediately while the lettuce is fresh and crunchy.

💡 Make the tuna-avocado mix on the day you eat it; it keeps chilled for 24 hours pressed under cling film with extra lemon, but browns beyond that. Wash and dry lettuce leaves ahead and box separately.
💡 Drain the tuna thoroughly and press out the water with the back of a spoon, otherwise the avocado mixture goes sloppy and soaks through the lettuce cups within minutes.
Add the orange and lemon sections to the blender.
Add the carrot and ginger next.
Pour in water and add ice.
Blend on high for 60 seconds or until the texture becomes smooth and bright.
Strain for a light juice or enjoy with pulp for added fiber and fullness.

💡 Blend to order if possible; strained juice keeps 24 hours in a full, sealed bottle but separates and loses its brightness. Freeze orange segments and carrot in one bag for a quick post-training version.
💡 Peel the orange fully and remove the white pith and any pips, which turn the juice bitter in a blender. Whisk the whey into the water before the fruit so it dissolves rather than foaming on top.
Add mango and banana to the blender first for a sweet, smooth base.
Add spinach and coconut water. Blend on medium to combine.
Increase to high speed and blend until creamy and no leafy chunks remain.
Stir in chia seeds and pulse a few times to distribute evenly.
Pour into glasses for a tropical, hydrating smoothie.
💡 Freeze spinach in muffin-tin pucks with a splash of coconut water so each portion drops straight into the jug. Blended, it keeps 24 hours chilled; the chia will thicken it, so loosen with water.
💡 Blend the spinach with the coconut water and whey first until no flecks remain, then add the frozen mango and banana; cold fruit added first traps the leaves above the blades.
In a food processor, combine almonds and dates; pulse until finely chopped.
Add cinnamon, nutmeg, chia seeds, coconut oil, and vanilla. Blend until sticky dough forms.
Roll into bite-sized balls and refrigerate for 30 minutes before serving.
💡 Keep in an airtight box in the fridge for two weeks or freeze for three months in a single layer; they are pleasant eaten straight from the freezer without thawing.
💡 If the dates are dry, soak them in warm water for 10 minutes and squeeze out before processing; otherwise the dough will not bind and the balls crumble. Chill the mixture 10 minutes before rolling.
Add the peach slices and banana to the blender.
Pour in the almond milk and add the vanilla extract.
Blend on high for 30–40 seconds until smooth and velvety.
Add the honey and blend again for a beautifully balanced sweetness.
Serve chilled for a bright, calming morning drink.
💡 Freeze the peach slices and banana together on a tray then bag them; a frozen portion blends thick and needs no ice. If chilling a blended batch, drink within 24 hours.
💡 Honey sinks and sticks to the jug when added last on high speed, so stir it into the almond milk with the vanilla and whey before the fruit goes in.
Add kiwi and cucumber to the blender first for a crisp, fresh base.
Pour in coconut water and blend on medium to start softening the ingredients.
Add ice and blend on high until smooth and chilled.
Taste and add honey if a slightly sweeter note is desired.
Pour into glasses and enjoy a refreshing, hydrating drink.
💡 Kiwi turns bitter and cucumber goes watery on standing, so this is a blend-and-drink smoothie; do not batch it. Pre-portion peeled kiwi and cucumber chunks in the freezer for up to a month.
💡 Peel the kiwis completely and remove the hard white core; skin and core give a fuzzy, bitter texture even on high speed. Over-blending the seeds also turns it bitter, so stop as soon as smooth.
In a food processor, combine oats, coconut, and matcha until fine.
Add almond butter, honey, and vanilla; blend until a sticky dough forms.
Roll into balls and chill for 30 minutes before serving.
💡 Store in a sealed tub in the fridge for 10 days or freeze for two months; matcha fades with light, so keep them in a dark box. Let frozen balls stand 10 minutes before eating.

💡 Process the oats and coconut until they resemble coarse flour before adding almond butter; large oat flakes stop the dough binding. If it will not hold, add 3.5 g of honey rather than more nut butter.
Add pineapple and cucumber chunks to your blender.
Pour in water to help everything liquefy smoothly.
Add ice to chill and lighten the texture.
Blend on high for 45–60 seconds until the mixture becomes completely liquid.
If you prefer a clearer juice, strain it through a fine-mesh sieve; if you enjoy fiber, leave it unstrained.
💡 Fresh pineapple contains an enzyme that keeps working after blending, so the juice goes flat and slightly fizzy by day two; drink within 24 hours, well chilled, and shake first.
💡 Give the whey and water a short low blast on their own before adding pineapple and cucumber; whey tipped over the fruit at high speed makes a stiff foam that sits on top.
Add chopped apples, celery, and cucumber to the blender.
Pour in cold water and add lemon juice.
Blend on medium for 30 seconds, then high until smooth and liquid.
Strain through a fine mesh strainer if you prefer a clear juice, or leave as-is for fiber.
Serve over ice and enjoy a crisp, detoxifying drink.
💡 Apple browns within minutes of blending, so the lemon is essential; even so, drink within 12 hours in a bottle filled to the brim. Apple and celery chunks can be frozen together for later.
💡 Strip the strings from the celery stalks with a peeler and core the apples; celery fibre wraps around the blades and shows up as threads in the finished juice.
Add blueberries and banana to the blender first for a smooth base.
Pour in almond milk and lemon juice. Blend on medium for 20–30 seconds.
Increase speed to high and blend until fully smooth and creamy.
Add ice and blend briefly for a chilled texture.
Pour immediately and enjoy a tangy, antioxidant-rich drink.
💡 Freeze the blueberries and banana together in one bag so the smoothie comes out thick without ice. If blending ahead, keep chilled up to 24 hours; the lemon slows browning.
💡 Acid poured onto undissolved whey leaves grainy specks, so blend the whey and almond milk first, then the fruit, and add the lemon juice last with the ice for a smooth finish.
Add the orange and lemon segments into the blender.
Add the sliced cucumber and mint leaves.
Pour in the water and blend until smooth and bright.
Strain through a fine sieve for a clearer, more refreshing texture.
Serve immediately for maximum vitamin freshness.
💡 Mint blackens and turns bitter once blended, so this juice is best drunk within a couple of hours; if you must keep it, strain first and refrigerate for up to 24 hours.
💡 Add the mint leaves with stems removed and blend briefly on medium rather than a long high-speed run; over-processing pulverises the leaves and gives a grassy, bitter note.
Add all berries and pineapple into the blender first to create a fruity base.
Pour in almond milk and blend on medium for 20–30 seconds.
Increase speed to high until smooth and creamy.
Add chia seeds and pulse briefly to distribute evenly.
Pour into glasses and enjoy a vibrant, immunity-boosting smoothie.

💡 Bag strawberries, blueberries and pineapple in single portions and freeze; a frozen portion produces a thick smoothie without ice. Chia thickens it in the fridge, so blend and drink within a few hours.
💡 Hull the strawberries and trim any woody pineapple core; both leave fibrous bits that a domestic blender cannot break down. Pulse the chia in for only a few seconds to keep the texture loose.
Chop carrots into small pieces and add to the blender first.
Add the orange segments and grated ginger.
Pour in water and add ice. Blend on medium for 30 seconds, then high until fully liquefied.
Strain for a smooth juice, or leave as-is for extra fiber.
Serve immediately for a vibrant, immunity-boosting drink.
💡 Strain it straight after blending if batching; unstrained pulp separates into a sludge within hours. Keeps 24 hours in a sealed bottle, and carrot pieces freeze well for two months.
💡 Cut the carrot into pieces no bigger than 1 cm and run the medium stage for the full 30 seconds before high; big chunks bounce on the blades and leave grit in the juice.
Add the pineapple chunks and banana to your blender.
Drop in the peeled piece of ginger — if you prefer a milder flavor, slice it thinly before adding.
Pour in the cold water and squeeze in the lemon juice.
Blend on high for 30–45 seconds until everything becomes liquid and vibrant yellow.
If you want a thinner, juice-like drink, strain through a sieve; if you prefer it thicker, serve as-is.
Pour immediately into glasses for maximum freshness.
💡 Pineapple juice ferments faster than most, so drink this within 24 hours and keep it in a full, sealed bottle. Freeze pineapple chunks and banana together to skip the ice next time.
💡 Whole ginger pieces survive a 30-second blend and give a fiery bite in one mouthful, so grate it finely or slice it thin as the recipe suggests, and add it below the fruit near the blades.
Add melon chunks and cucumber slices to the blender.
Pour in cold water and add the lime juice.
Blend on medium first to break down the melon, then switch to high for 30–40 seconds until smooth.
Add ice and blend briefly for a chilled texture.
Taste and adjust lime or water for the perfect refreshing balance.
💡 Melon and cucumber give up water as they sit, so this thins and separates within hours; blend and drink straight away. Freeze cubed melon on a tray then bag for cold portions without ice.
💡 Deseed the melon and scrape the watery seed core out of the cucumber; both make the drink insipid and foamy. Add lime at the end and taste, as melon sweetness varies wildly.
Chop the apple into smaller chunks and add to the blender.
Add the sliced ginger for a sharper, cleaner blend.
Pour in the water and blend until completely smooth.
Strain through a fine mesh strainer to remove pulp and collect the clear juice.
Stir in the lemon juice and serve over ice for a refreshing, immune-boosting drink.
💡 Strained apple juice browns fast, so add the lemon straight after straining and drink within 12 hours; a sealed bottle filled to the top helps. Apple chunks can be frozen for future batches.
💡 Whisk the whey into the clear juice after straining rather than before; otherwise most of it stays in the pulp in the sieve and your protein goes in the bin.
